For example, if we join using the case_id variable, all other variables in the resulting combined dataset will be named something like country.x and country.y. The .x and .y suffixes differentiate the country columns from the rookies dataset and the veterans dataset, respectively. However, if you’re certain that columns with the same name in both datasets also contain the same values, or if you simply don’t want to retain both versions in the output, there are a couple of approaches to prevent or remove the duplicate columns with the .x and .y suffixes: 1. Using the by argument: The by argument in the join functions lets you specify which columns to join by. By creating a character vector of the column names in your data frames, you can provide this column name vector to the by argument. This way, you’re specifying to join on all columns in your data frames. Since the column names and values are identical in both data frames, dplyr won’t create the duplicate columns with .x and .y suffixes. column_names <- colnames(rookies) # colnames() grabs the column names from the rookies data frame and turns them into a character vector full_joined <- full_join(rookies, veterans, by = column_names) full_joined ## # A tibble: 1,169 × 16 ## country reach employment temp_contract autonomy_selection autonomy_emphasis ## <fct> <fct> <chr> <fct> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 Germany Nati… Full-time Permanent 5 4 ## 2 Germany Nati… Full-time Permanent 3 4 ## 3 Switzerl… Regi… Full-time Permanent 4 4 ## 4 Switzerl… Local Part-time Permanent 4 5 ## 5 Denmark Nati… Full-time Permanent 3 3 ## 6 Denmark Nati… Full-time Permanent 2 4 ## 7 Austria Local Full-time Permanent 5 5 ## 8 UK Regi… Full-time Permanent 3 4 ## 9 UK Tran… Full-time Permanent 4 5 ## 10 UK Tran… Full-time Permanent 4 4 ## # ℹ 1,159 more rows ## # ℹ 10 more variables: ethics_1 <dbl>, ethics_2 <dbl>, ethics_3 <dbl>, ## # ethics_4 <dbl>, work_experience <dbl>, trust_parliament <dbl>, ## # trust_government <dbl>, trust_parties <dbl>, trust_politicians <dbl>, ## # case_id <int> You receive only 16 columns in your combined data set. Renaming .x columns and dropping .y columns: Using the knowledge that you’ll acquire in the next few tutorials, you could also rename all the .x columns in your combined data set and delete all .y columns. inner_joined <- inner_joined %>% rename_with(~ gsub("\\.x$", "", .), everything()) %>% # replaces all column endings ".x" with nothing: "" select(-matches("\\.y$")) # deselects all columns that end with ".y" inner_joined ## # A tibble: 117 × 16 ## country reach employment temp_contract autonomy_selection autonomy_emphasis ## <fct> <fct> <chr> <fct> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 Germany Nati… Full-time Permanent 5 4 ## 2 Denmark Nati… Full-time Permanent 3 3 ## 3 UK Regi… Full-time Permanent 3 4 ## 4 UK Tran… Full-time Permanent 4 4 ## 5 UK Regi… Full-time Permanent 4 4 ## 6 Germany Local Full-time Permanent 4 5 ## 7 UK Regi… Full-time Permanent 4 4 ## 8 Switzerl… Regi… Freelancer <NA> 2 3 ## 9 Denmark Regi… Full-time Temporary 3 3 ## 10 Austria Nati… Full-time Permanent 3 4 ## # ℹ 107 more rows ## # ℹ 10 more variables: ethics_1 <dbl>, ethics_2 <dbl>, ethics_3 <dbl>, ## # ethics_4 <dbl>, work_experience <dbl>, trust_parliament <dbl>, ## # trust_government <dbl>, trust_parties <dbl>, trust_politicians <dbl>, ## # case_id <int> You are left with only 16 columns. 3. We will create a fictional dataset based on the Worlds of Journalism (WoJ) dataset, with a twist - it will have several panel waves. Imagine that the WoJ dataset has been expanded to include data from different years: set.seed(123) WoJ_panel <- WoJ %>% slice_sample(n = 10) %>% select(case_id, work_experience, autonomy_selection) %>% mutate( work_experience_w2018 = work_experience + sample(1:1, 10, replace = TRUE), work_experience_w2019 = work_experience_w2018 + sample(1:1, 10, replace = TRUE), autonomy_selection_w2018 = autonomy_selection + sample(-1:1, 10, replace = TRUE), autonomy_selection_w2019 = autonomy_selection_w2018 + sample(-1:1, 10, replace = TRUE) ) %>% select(-c(work_experience, autonomy_selection)) WoJ_panel ## # A tibble: 10 × 5 ## case_id work_experience_w2018 work_experience_w2019 autonomy_selection_w2018 ## <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 415 24 25 3 ## 2 463 5 6 4 ## 3 179 26 27 4 ## 4 526 38 39 3 ## 5 195 13 14 5 ## 6 938 26 27 4 ## 7 1142 4 5 3 ## 8 1038 10 11 6 ## 9 665 16 17 2 ## 10 602 3 4 1 ## # ℹ 1 more variable: autonomy_selection_w2019 <dbl> 7.3.1 pivot_longer() Let’s say you want to analyze how work experience and autonomy selection change over time. Exercise 5: Advanced data management (optional) NOTE: This part of the tutorial is not your typical beginner material — it covers some more advanced topics. The exercise is therefore OPTIONAL and is intended as a resource you can return to once you are ready to learn and apply these advanced data operations to your own projects. I do not expect you to complete these exercises during the beginner’s course. After working through this exercise, you’ll… import and combine several files without copying and pasting code; clean inconsistent variable names before combining datasets; choose an appropriate dplyr join for a research question; reshape data from wide to long format and back again; select variables with tidyselect helpers; select observations with stringr::str_detect(); combine several advanced data-management steps in one workflow. For this exercise, we will work with fictional survey data created specifically for this course. None of the files contain real respondents. Download the practice-data package and unzip it into the root folder of your R Project. Keep the folder structure unchanged. After unzipping, you should have a folder called: advanced_practice Before starting, load the packages that we need: library(tidyverse) Task 1 The folder advanced_practice/multiple_files contains three semicolon-separated CSV files. All three files contain the same variables, but each file contains different respondents. Your goal is to combine them into one data frame without importing the files one by one. Save the relative folder path in an object called path. Use list.files() to find all CSV files in the folder. Store their full relative paths in file_paths. Use map() and read.csv2() to read all files. Combine all files with bind_rows() and save the result as combined_data. Inspect your combined_data object. Questions: - How many respondents are contained in the combined dataset? - How many variables are contained in the combined dataset? Task 2 Real research data are not always perfectly standardized. The folder advanced_practice/multiple_files_messy contains three additional CSV files. They are supposed to contain the same variables, but their column names are inconsistent. Do not manually edit the CSV files. Fix the problem in R. Create a vector called messy_paths containing all CSV file paths in this folder. Read all files with map() and read.csv2(). Use check.names = FALSE so that R does not automatically modify the inconsistent headers before you clean them yourself. Before combining them, standardize the column names so that they are: lowercase; free of leading or trailing spaces; written with underscores instead of spaces. Combine the cleaned files with bind_rows() and save the result as combined_messy. Inspect the resulting combined_messy object. Question: - Determine how many missing values occur in trust_government? Hint: The following Base R functions may help when cleaning names: tolower(), trimws(), and gsub(). If you need help, you can always use help(), e.g., help(tolower()) and look in the tutorial section! Copying code is intended! Task 3 The folder advanced_practice/joins contains two datasets: journalist_profiles.csv contains demographic and employment information; journalist_attitudes.csv contains attitude measures. Import both files as profiles and attitudes. Both datasets use respondent_id as their unique identifier, but they do not contain exactly the same respondents. Create four new datasets by joining profiles and attitudes with: inner_join() left_join() right_join() full_join() Before running the joins, predict which join you would use if you wanted to: keep only respondents contained in both datasets; keep every respondent from profiles; keep every respondent from attitudes; keep every respondent contained in either dataset. Bonus: Use anti_join() to identify respondents that appear in profiles but not in attitudes. Task 4 The file advanced_practice/panel/journalist_panel_wide.csv contains fictional measurements from two survey waves. Import the file as panel_wide and inspect its structure. The variables follow a naming pattern such as: autonomy_selection_w1 autonomy_selection_w2 trust_government_w1 trust_government_w2 Use pivot_longer() to transform the dataset into a long format with the following columns: respondent_id country measure wave score Store the result as panel_long. Hint: You can use names_to = c("measure", "wave") together with names_pattern. Next, transform panel_long back into wide format with pivot_wider() and store the result as panel_wide_again. Task 5 Return to combined_data from Task 1. Solve the following tasks with select() and tidyselect helpers: 1. Select respondent_id and all variables whose names start with "autonomy". 2. Select all numeric variables. 3. Select all character variables. 4. Reorder the complete dataset so that respondent_id, country, and employment appear first, followed by all remaining variables. Then use filter() and str_detect() to: 5. select all freelancers; 6. select all employment categories whose labels end in "time"; 7. select everyone who is either a freelancer or whose employment category ends in "time". Task 6 Now combine several of the techniques from this chapter. Starting with the two datasets from Task 3: 1. join profiles and attitudes so that all respondents from either dataset are retained; 2. keep respondent_id, country, employment, work_experience, and all variables whose names start with "autonomy", plus trust_government; 3. keep only respondents for whom employment is available; 4. keep only freelancers or employment categories ending in "time"; 5. group the data by country; 6. calculate the mean of autonomy_selection and trust_government, removing missing values; 7. also calculate the number of respondents in each country; 8. arrange the result alphabetically by country.
